notes.meaning: Israel finished its long wandering in the wilderness and set up camp in the low plains across the Jordan River from Jericho. This land had once belonged to Moab before another king took it, but Israel now held it after their recent victories. They were now at the doorstep of the land God had promised them.
Balak, the ruler of Moab, watched everything Israel had done to the Amorites. He knew that the Amorite armies were powerful, so Israel's total defeat of them filled him with great dread.

The people of Moab were filled with deep panic and sick with fear because Israel had so many people. In truth, Moab did not need to fear, because God had told Israel not to attack them. Their terror came from a guilty conscience and their own refusal to trust God.

Moab turned to the leaders of neighboring Midian to make a partnership against Israel. Balak warned them that this massive crowd would strip the land bare, just as an ox eats every blade of grass in a pasture. Rather than seeking peace or thanking God for defeating their old Amorite enemies, Moab plotted to destroy God's people.

Balak sent messengers hundreds of miles away to Pethor near the Euphrates River to hire Balaam. Balaam was a well-known diviner, someone who practiced pagan rituals to foretell the future or speak curses. Balak complained that a huge nation had come out of Egypt and was now crowding his border.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Archaeologists found an ancient wall inscription at Deir Alla in Jordan that names Balaam son of Beor, confirming he was widely known in the ancient Near East as a seer who received visions at night.

notes.meaning: Balak begged Balaam to put a spiritual curse on Israel so Moab might defeat them in battle. In the ancient world, kings believed a sorcerer could call on the gods to abandon an enemy army and ruin them. Balak believed Balaam held total power to decide who was blessed and who was cursed.

The messengers from Moab and Midian set out carrying payment for Balaam's services. These fees were customary for fortune-tellers, and Balaam was a man who loved money. When they arrived, they gave him Balak's urgent message.

Balaam told the princes to spend the night while he waited to hear what the LORD said. He knew the name of the true God of Israel, but he should have turned the men away immediately rather than entertaining an evil request. Lingering to talk with temptation puts any person in great danger of falling.

God appeared to Balaam in the night and asked him who the visitors were. God already knew who they were, but He asked the question to make Balaam face the wickedness of the errand. It gave Balaam an opportunity to admit his own greedy motives.

Balaam told God that the king of Moab had sent for him to put a curse on a great multitude coming out of Egypt. He explained that Balak hoped this curse would give Moab the power to drive Israel out of the region. Balaam accurately reported the errand, but he hid the flattering words Balak had used to praise his power.

God gave Balaam an absolute command not to go with the men and not to curse Israel. God explained that these people were already blessed by Him, and His blessing could never be overturned. An attempt to curse those whom God has chosen brings God's own judgment upon the one who curses.

Balaam got up the next morning and told Balak's princes to return home because the LORD would not give him permission to go. He obeyed on the surface, but his words showed he secretly wished he could go. By failing to mention that God had declared Israel blessed forever, he left the door open for Balak to try again.

The princes returned to Balak and reported simply that Balaam refused to come. They failed to tell their king that the LORD Himself had forbidden it. This made Balak think Balaam was only holding out for more honor and higher pay.

Balak did not give up, but sent a second group of leaders that was larger and held higher royal rank. Sinful people will often spare no effort or expense to accomplish their evil plans. Balak believed he could win Balaam over by appealing to his pride.

The new messengers came to Balaam and urged him to let nothing stand in his way. Balak was telling him to ignore every obstacle, including conscience, fear, and even God's commands. Worldly temptations often press us to act as though God's laws do not matter.

Balak promised to reward Balaam with great riches and royal promotion, offering to do anything Balaam asked. In exchange, he repeated his demand that Balaam come and curse Israel. Balak laid a trap designed to feed both Balaam's love of money and his thirst for status.

Balaam answered that he could not disobey the LORD his God for a palace filled with gold and silver. His words sounded deeply righteous and faithful, but his heart still longed for the money. Speaking pious words is easy, but God looks directly at what is inside a person's heart.

Balaam asked this second group of men to spend the night so he could see what else God might say. This was an act of rebellion, because God had already given him a clear and final answer. Asking God for permission to do what He has already forbidden reveals a heart controlled by sin.

God came to Balaam that night and told him he could go with the men, but only speak what God commanded him. God's permission was not an approval of Balaam's greed, but a judgment that handed him over to his own stubborn desires. God sometimes lets wicked people pursue their foolish wishes in order to bring about His own holy purposes.
